claim: The AWS caching best practices say to always apply a time to live (TTL) to all your cache keys, except those you update by write-through caching.
question: Which cache keys should get a TTL according to the AWS caching best practices?

values.display: Always apply a time to live (TTL) to all of your cache keys
except those you are updating by write-through caching

evidence.quote: Always apply a time to live (TTL) to all of your cache keys, except those you are updating by write-through caching.

claim: For rapidly changing data such as comments, leaderboards or activity streams, the AWS caching best practices suggest setting a short TTL of a few seconds instead of write-through caching or complex expiration logic.
question: What does AWS suggest for caching rapidly changing data?

values.display: set a short TTL of a few seconds
rapidly changing data such as comments, leaderboards, or activity streams

evidence.quote: For rapidly changing data such as comments, leaderboards, or activity streams, rather than adding write-through caching or complex expiration logic, just set a short TTL of a few seconds.

claim: Apply a lazy caching strategy anywhere in your app where data is read often but written infrequently.
question: For which data does AWS recommend lazy caching?

values.display: read often, but written infrequently
apply a lazy caching strategy

evidence.quote: You should apply a lazy caching strategy anywhere in your app where you have data that is going to be read often, but written infrequently.

claim: A good use of write-through caching is any type of aggregate, such as a top 100 game leaderboard, the top 10 most popular news stories or recommendations.

values.display: any type of aggregate
a top 100 game leaderboard

evidence.quote: A good example is any type of aggregate, such as a top 100 game leaderboard, or the top 10 most popular news stories, or even recommendations.

claim: Lazy caching catches cache misses on reads and write-through caching populates data on writes, so the two approaches complement each other.
question: Why combine lazy caching with write-through caching?

values.display: Lazy caching catches cache misses on reads
write-through caching populates data on writes

evidence.quote: Lazy caching catches cache misses on reads, and write-through caching populates data on writes, so the two approaches complement each other.

claim: Write-through caching can fill the cache with unnecessary objects that are never accessed, and it can cause lots of cache churn if certain records are updated repeatedly.
question: What are the disadvantages of write-through caching according to the AWS caching best practices?

values.display: filled with unnecessary objects
lots of cache churn

evidence.quote: The cache can be filled with unnecessary objects that aren't actually being accessed.
It can result in lots of cache churn if certain records are updated repeatedly.

values.display: a centralized session management data store is the ideal solution
better session durability when your fleet of web servers is elastic

evidence.quote: With modern application architectures, utilizing a centralized session management data store is the ideal solution for a number of reasons including providing, consistent user experiences across all web servers, better session durability when your fleet of web servers is elastic and higher availability when session data is replicated across cache servers.

claim: A cache that is resident on the same node as the application can lose integrity when application nodes are scaled in and out, so a separate shared cache layer suits systems with dynamic scaling.
question: Why not keep the cache on the application node when the fleet scales in and out?

values.display: scaling may affect the integrity of the cache
application nodes can be dynamically scaled in and out

evidence.quote: This is especially relevant in a system where application nodes can be dynamically scaled in and out. If the cache is resident on the same node as the application or systems utilizing it, scaling may affect the integrity of the cache.

claim: A single cache instance can provide hundreds of thousands of IOPS, potentially replacing a number of database instances and so driving the total cost down.

values.display: hundreds of thousands of IOPS
potentially replacing a number of database instances

evidence.quote: A single cache instance can provide hundreds of thousands of IOPS (Input/output operations per second), potentially replacing a number of database instances, thus driving the total cost down.

claim: Storing common keys in an in-memory cache mitigates the need to overprovision database resources for hot spots, while giving fast and predictable performance for the most commonly accessed data.
question: How does a cache help with database hot spots?

values.display: mitigates the need to overprovision
most commonly accessed data

evidence.quote: Storing common keys in an in-memory cache mitigates the need to overprovision while providing fast and predictable performance for the most commonly accessed data.

claim: Memory is orders of magnitude faster than disk, so reading data from an in-memory cache is extremely fast, at sub-millisecond latency.
question: How fast is reading from an in-memory cache compared with disk?

values.display: orders of magnitude faster than disk
sub-millisecond

evidence.quote: Because memory is orders of magnitude faster than disk (magnetic or SSD), reading data from in-memory cache is extremely fast (sub-millisecond).

claim: The Well-Architected Framework says systems should either not require state or offload state, so that there is no dependence on locally stored data between requests; this allows servers to be replaced at will without an availability impact.
question: Why does Well-Architected recommend making systems stateless?

values.display: offload state
servers to be replaced at will without causing an availability impact

evidence.quote: Systems should either not require state, or should offload state such that between different client requests, there is no dependence on locally stored data on disk and in memory. This allows servers to be replaced at will without causing an availability impact.

claim: Stateless applications can scale horizontally because any of the available compute resources, such as EC2 instances and Lambda functions, can service any request.
question: Why can stateless applications scale horizontally?

values.display: scale horizontally
any of the available compute resources

evidence.quote: In addition to server replacement, another benefit of stateless applications is that they can scale horizontally because any of the available compute resources (such as EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions) can service any request.
